hn-50563148.t: Claude solves two open problems in the physics of black holes
hn-50563148.s: Claude Fable 5.2 has solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes and the search for a theory of quantum gravity.
ex: Modern physics rests on two frameworks: general relativity and quantum mechanics. General relativity describes very large things, like stars; quantum mechanics describes very small things, such as atoms. Both are astonishingly good at predicting how the universe behaves, but they’re mathematically incompatible. Finding a theory that unites them—“quantum gravity”—is one of the field’s biggest goals. Black holes are a natural testing ground, because they’re one of the few areas where both relativity and quantum mechanics matter—they pack immense mass into a very small space. One of the most useful tools for studying quantum gravity is called holographic duality. The real universe has three dimensions of space and one of time, which relativity combines into four-dimensional spacetime. But physicists studying quantum gravity often work with simpler model universes that they can understand in more detail.

hn-50561508.s: Pete Warden on Local AI, Open Models, Voice Interfaces, and the Future of Hardware. Subscribe: Apple • Spotify • Overcast … More
ex: Pete Warden, co-creator of Moonshine Voice and a longtime deep learning engineer, joins me to discuss why AI increasingly wants to run locally rather than in the cloud. We explore the rapid progress of open-weight models, what it takes to run AI on laptops and in browsers, and how low-latency speech models could make voice a more natural interface. We also discuss specialized versus end-to-end models, the economics of local AI, and emerging hardware approaches that could challenge today’s GPU-centric infrastructure. [This episode originally aired on Generative AI in the Real World, a podcast series I’m hosting for O’Reilly.] Ben Lorica. All right. Today we have an old friend, Pete Warden of Useful Sensors, and their main website is actually at moonshine.ai. If you go to the website, you’ll see that they’re very much about voice on-device, and we will definitely talk to Pete about all things speech and all things edge computing.

hn-50559749.t: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
hn-50559749.s: Foolscap uses AI to help you write, without writing for you. Foolscap does not generate text for you. Your writing is entirely yours.
ex: A writing app that knows your whole book. As you write, it notices what connects and what's left hanging, and shows you where, in your own words. It never writes a word for you. Your writing is never used to train AI. Mark a book private, and nothing of it goes to any AI at all. People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here. It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work.

hn-50554374.t: Gemini 4 Neon looks like an Opus 5.5 competitor
hn-50554374.s: TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5 Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if…
ex: TLDR: we project Gemini 4 Neon’s performance based on what a faster Gemini 4 Carbon might score and find it equivalent to Opus 5.5 Gemini 4 Carbon is the best model on the Agent Duel leaderboard if you exclude early voting. Carbon’s main problem is that it is slooooow. Today, Gemini 4 Neon was released, and looks to be an incremental benchmark improvement with a very large speed improvement. Earlier today, it was being served extremely fast via OpenRouter: 127 tokens per second. This is way faster than Carbon at 46 tokens per second. This got me wondering, could Neon be not just a good model but the best model? To investigate, I modeled the win rate in our leaderboard. The best model has three components, model identity, speed and whether the user voted early. My initial modeling did poorly, so I added an interaction between speed and early voting. This ended up working well. And surprisingly, speed seems to be pretty much as important as model identity (another blog on that soon).

hn-50560461.t: OpenAI still has a WebRTC Problem
hn-50560461.s: Media over QUIC: Your voice AI keeps asking "can you repeat that?" because WebRTC throws away your words. MoQ dun do that.
ex: On a previous episode, I flamed OpenAI for using WebRTC and it went viral on Hacker News. A huge shoutout to Sean DuBois and Justin Uberti (WebRTC experts at OpenAI) for reaching out after my unhinged rant. You could have just said @kixelated ur dumb but you didn’t. Alas, my divinely anointed crusade against WebRTC is not over. deus vult Let’s say you’re a vibe coder at a frontier lab working on a voice AI product. Let’s say you’re making (and burning) an obscene amount of cash. Let’s say one of your users vocalizes: what is le capital of France? You boot up your favorite application: ChatGPT™. You click on the microphone and grunt: OH NO, hypothetical sudden packet loss. A kraken nibbles on some underwater cable. All too common I’m afraid. WebRTC is designed for conference calls, aka real humans and real voices. It is hyper aggressive and will drop any late audio packets to keep latency real-time. Just like Leonardo DiCaprio, anything above 30ms is too old.

hn-50559719.t: Making 8-page foldable zines from a single A4 sheet in the browser
hn-50559719.s: A small update on fanzines.app: designing in real spreads, batch photo drops, printer-safe margins, and support for English and Spanish.
ex: A few months ago, I wrote about how I started giving away zines to my friends, my family, and people at work. If you've never made one, the fold is simple. Take a single A4 sheet of paper, fold it in half three times, open it back up, and cut along the center crease with scissors. Fold the sheet into a cross and close it, and you have an 8-page booklet with no staples or glue. I fill mine with whatever I feel like printing: photos, poems, or notes. The part I never liked was laying out the flat sheet on the computer before printing. Because the A4 paper folds back on itself, the pages sit in a strange order and the top row has to be upside down: I got tired of rotating pictures and double-checking columns in Photoshop every time I wanted to print a new zine, so I built fanzines.app. In the browser, you lay out each page right-side up with photos and text. When you export, the app places all 8 panels onto the A4 grid with the top row rotated 180 degrees and generates a 300 DPI PDF.

gh-1462995598.s: From a 30 fps console stream to 60–120 fps on your PC. · frame-interpolation · frame-generation · nvidia · windows · dlss · super-resolution · vulkan · dlss5 · upscaling · rife · neural-rendering ·…
ex: frameglide streams your console to your Windows PC and draws new frames between the ones the game sends, live — a 30 fps game plays at 60, 90 or up to 120 fps to match your screen, sharpened to fit it. Nothing gets installed on the console, and the tool is free and open source. [download-url]: https://github.com/bothaggsigym1988/frameglide/releases Change everything on the Settings page or press M in the video window; Auto-detect picks the best for your PC and explains each choice. The picture stays black, or the console says the content can't be shown — turn off HDCP on the console (Settings → System → HDMI on a PS5), connect again, and turn it back on for video apps afterwards. Does it change anything on my console? No. Nothing is installed on the console; your PC receives the Remote Play stream like the maker's own app does. Does it work with AMD or Intel graphics cards?
